title: Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. (June 1992 TCC) Ruling
subject: Agricultural company SR&ED appeal evaluating whether greenhouse cultivation experiments qualified for tax credits.
outcome: Appeal allowed in part; court recognized systematic agricultural testing as SR&ED while denying routine farming costs.
summary: Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. v. Minister of National Revenue, decided by the Tax Court of Canada in 1992, held that SR&ED claimants selling experimental production need not deduct sales proceeds from qualified expenditures when calculating investment tax credits under the Income Tax Act. The Court rejected the Minister's netting approach and allowed the oyster mushroom producer's appeal with costs.
metaDescription: Discover the June 1992 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED ruling for Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. on Canadian R&D tax incentives.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural History and Factual Matrix

In Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. v. Minister of National Revenue (rendered in the original French trial record as Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. c. Ministre du Revenu national), Docket 89-2514(IT), reported at [1992] T.C.J. No. 370, 93 D.T.C. 597 and 93 D.T.C. 603 (the English-language reasons being a translation from the original French), the Tax Court of Canada adjudicated a foundational dispute in the administration of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive regime. Heard in Montreal, Quebec, on March 13, 1992, with formal judgment handed down on June 17, 1992, by the Honourable Judge Louise Lamarre Proulx, the appeal arose from an assessment issued by the Minister of National Revenue (then operating through Revenue Canada, now the Canada Revenue Agency or CRA) for the appellant's 1986 taxation year.

The appellant, Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc., was a company specializing in the production of oyster mushrooms (pleurotes) which, according to the Minister's pleadings, also carried on a business of purchasing and reselling mushrooms. While the sale of oyster mushrooms generated the appellant's revenue—mushrooms from its experimental production accounting for 80 percent of its total sales of $121,224 in 1986—the corporation concurrently undertook a scientific research and experimental development project, recognized as such by Revenue Canada, aimed at finding a process for achieving a constant and continuing production of oyster mushrooms; according to the Minister's pleadings, 80 percent of the appellant's activities were oriented toward this research. Specifically, the appellant developed an experimental oyster mushroom production process whose purpose was to control and limit the spread of oyster mushroom spores; its technique consisted in covering the inside of its building with metal slats and covering logs of wood with perforated plastic bags, the mushrooms growing out of the logs at the perforated places.

For its 1986 taxation year, Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. claimed a research and development Investment Tax Credit (ITC) of $55,710 in respect of the expenditures incurred in its SR&ED project. Upon audit, the Minister of National Revenue assessed the taxpayer across two primary dimensions. First, while Revenue Canada agreed that 80 percent of the appellant's current expenditures (that is, $85,104) related to research and development—the same percentage the appellant used in its financial statements—the Minister applied that 80 percent proportion to the appellant's capital expenditures, concluded that they were not "all or substantially all" attributable to SR&ED, and excluded them (up to a maximum of $34,777) from the ITC calculation on the ground that the property was in fact used for production. Second, and of enduring significance for Canadian tax jurisprudence, the Minister applied an administrative policy known as the "netting" approach, reducing the $85,104 of qualifying current SR&ED expenditures by the $96,979 of income from the sale of the oyster mushrooms obtained from the experimental production, which left no qualified current expenditures on which to calculate the ITC.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The dispute in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. was governed by the interlocking provisions of the Canadian Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, as amended by S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, as applicable to the 1986 taxation year, hereinafter the "ITA") and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "ITR").

Under paragraph 37(1)(a) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada is entitled to deduct in computing income from the business for the year all amounts of a current nature expended on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer. Alternatively, at the taxpayer's option, those current SR&ED expenditures may be retained in an undeducted SR&ED expenditure pool to be carried forward and deducted in subsequent taxation years. Paragraph 37(7)(b) of the ITA delegates the substantive definition of "scientific research and experimental development" to the ITR, while clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A) of the ITA, as then in force, stipulates that references to expenditures on or in respect of scientific research (where they occur other than in subsection 37(2)) include expenditures each of which was incurred for, and "all or substantially all" (interpreted administratively and judicially as 90 percent or more) of which was attributable to, the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, with clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(B) separately covering current expenditures directly attributable, as determined by regulation, to that prosecution.

The tax credit mechanism operates through subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, which permit a taxpayer to deduct an Investment Tax Credit from Part I tax otherwise payable, calculated as a statutory percentage of the taxpayer's "qualified expenditure" (20 percent for general claims in the relevant period, and 35 percent under subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA in the calculation applicable to the appellant), a portion of which may be refundable under section 127.1 of the ITA. Subsection 127(9) defines a "qualified expenditure" as an expenditure in respect of SR&ED made by a taxpayer after March 31, 1977, that qualifies as an expenditure described in paragraph 37(1)(a) or subparagraph 37(1)(b)(i), explicitly excluding "prescribed expenditures".

At the regulatory level, section 2900 of the ITR defines SR&ED for the purposes of Part XXIX of the Regulations and paragraph 37(7)(b) of the ITA as a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis," categorized into basic research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view), applied research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view), and development (use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes). Crucially, the concluding exclusions of section 2900 remove routine quality control, routine testing, and commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product—as well as the commercial use of a new or improved process—from the ambit of eligible SR&ED. Finally, paragraph 2902(a) of the ITR enumerates the current "prescribed expenditures" excluded from the ITC calculation base under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, targeting expenditures of a current nature in respect of the general administration or management of a business, while paragraph 2902(b) prescribes capital expenditures in respect of the acquisition of property, except those incurred for and all or substantially all attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED (or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for that prosecution).

cells: ITA Paragraph 37(1)(a)
Authorizes current-year deduction (or pooling) of current expenditures incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada related to the taxpayer's business.

Defined the current expenditures underlying the ITC claim; Revenue Canada agreed that 80 percent of the appellant's current expenditures ($85,104) related to research and development and did not contest the section 37 deductions.
ITA Clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A)

Restricts qualifying expenditures (where the references occur other than in s. 37(2)) to outlays incurred for and "all or substantially all" attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, with clause (B) covering current expenditures directly attributable to it.
Not cited in the decision; the "all or substantially all" dispute in the case concerned the appellant's capital expenditures and was decided under paragraph 2902(b) of the ITR.
ITA Subsections 127(5) & 127(9)
Establishes the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) deduction against Part I tax and defines "qualified expenditure" by cross-reference to s. 37(1)(a).
Determined the base upon which the appellant calculated its ITC claim and whether sales revenue from experimental production reduced that base.
ITR Section 2900
Defines SR&ED as systematic investigation or search in science or technology by experiment or analysis, excluding commercial production.

Invoked by the Minister (paragraph 2900(h)) to argue that a taxpayer selling its products is in a commercial production phase; the Court rejected this, as the same expenditures cannot relate both to the research phase and to commercial production. Revenue Canada did not question that the appellant conducted SR&ED.
ITR Paragraph 2902(a)
Prescribes certain current expenditures (those in respect of the general administration or management of a business) that are ineligible for ITC calculation under s. 127(9).

Cited by the Court among the provisions applicable to the netting issue; the Minister did not invoke it to restrict the current expenditures, 80 percent of which were agreed to relate to research. The allocation dispute turned instead on paragraph 2902(b) and the capital expenditures.

body.text: The Court's Final Holding and Jurisprudential Legacy

Judge Lamarre Proulx allowed the appeal of Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. with costs. On the evidentiary question of expenditure allocation, which concerned the appellant's capital expenditures, the Tax Court of Canada accepted the uncontradicted testimony of the appellant's president that the capital expenditures claimed as qualified were all incurred for the purposes of the research laboratory, and held that the Minister's application to those capital expenditures of the 80 percent proportion established for current expenditures was not based on the facts and could not be considered valid.

On the overarching legal issue of "netting," Judge Lamarre Proulx repudiated the Minister's reassessment methodology. The Court held that the sums received from the sale of experimental products do not have to be deducted in calculating the amount of qualified expenditures within the meaning of subsection 127(5) of the ITA. Because the ITA contains no statutory mechanism mandating or authorizing the netting of sales revenue against qualified expenditures—as counsel for the Minister conceded—and because Parliament, where it wished to exclude amounts from qualified expenditures, said so expressly in subsection 127(11.1) of the ITA (government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments, the latter not including payments received for experimental products), the Court rejected the Minister's "object of the Act," accounting-matching, and paragraph 2900(h) arguments, leaving the ITC calculation on the full qualified current expenditures intact.

The ruling in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. immediately became a foundational precedent in Canadian SR&ED tax litigation. Five years later, in Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, Docket 94-990(IT)G, (1997) 97 D.T.C. 724 (T.C.C.), Judge Donald Bowman noted that the taxpayer's objections had been filed after Judge Lamarre Proulx's decision in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. (although its counsel had been consulted about objecting before that decision), observing that nothing turned on the timing. In Consoltex, where Revenue Canada had considered both direct revenue "netting" and a "carve-out" methodology—whereby a portion of the SR&ED costs would be attributed to the cost of sales of experimental textile fabrics—and had assessed on an agreed formula premised on the carve-out, Judge Bowman expressly agreed with Judge Lamarre Proulx's decision on the netting point and separately rejected the carve-out method, noting that although it may superficially appear to be a modified version of netting, it rests on a fundamentally different premise and does not conform to the scheme and purpose of the SR&ED provisions.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

Although Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. ultimately prevailed before the Tax Court of Canada, the audit reassessment and subsequent litigation exposed four severe legal, operational, and evidentiary vulnerabilities that routinely trigger reassessment by the CRA. Analyzing both the taxpayer's operational vulnerabilities and the Crown's legal errors in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. is essential for structuring defensible SR&ED claims in Canada.
Commingling of Experimental Development and Commercial Production in Shared Facilities

The primary operational catalyst for the audit dispute in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. was the sale of the oyster mushrooms produced through the appellant's experimental research, within a business that also carried on commercial mushroom activities. Although the evidence showed that the capital expenditures claimed as qualified were all incurred for the purposes of a research laboratory, Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. sold the mushrooms yielded by its experimental production—representing 80 percent of its total 1986 sales of $121,224—while also carrying on the purchase and resale of mushrooms and commercial oyster mushroom production. As Judge Bowman observed in Consoltex Inc., where the research was done in the taxpayer's production facilities with no separate research facility and the larger part of the fabrics produced in the course of the research was sold, those two facts were the reason the matter came before the court; research in production facilities raises no discrete question of principle, but it makes it more difficult to draw a clear line between production and research.

In Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc., the taxpayer's experimental technique—covering the interior of its building with metal slats and covering wooden logs with perforated plastic bags in order to control and limit the spread of oyster mushroom spores—simultaneously yielded harvestable mushrooms that were sold. From the perspective of a tax auditor applying section 2900 of the ITR, this commingling creates an immediate presumption of routine "commercial production" rather than "experimental development". When a taxpayer fails to erect clear physical, temporal, or procedural boundaries between experimental trial batches and standard commercial inventory runs, the Minister routinely denies the entire expenditure pool on the ground that the taxpayer was merely engaging in commercial production by trial and error rather than a systematic investigation in a field of science or technology.
The Extrastatutory "Netting" and "Carve-Out" Doctrines Regarding Experimental Production

The central legal controversy in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. stemmed from the sale of the oyster mushrooms produced during the taxpayer's experimental runs. Revenue Canada maintained an administrative policy requiring that revenue obtained from the sale of prototypes, pilot plants, scrap, or experimental production be deducted ("netted") against SR&ED expenditures; in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc., the Minister applied it to reduce the qualified expenditures of a current nature for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, while not contesting the appellant's section 37 deductions. The Crown's underlying policy theory was that the SR&ED investment tax credit is economic assistance intended to stimulate research, available only where the taxpayer cannot finance its research with the proceeds of disposition, and not meant to subsidize experimental research that finances itself through the sale of its experimental production; the Crown also invoked the accounting principle of matching.

However, as Judge Lamarre Proulx determined—and as contemporary tax commentary and Judge Bowman in Consoltex Inc. confirmed—Revenue Canada's netting position suffered from a fatal legal defect: there is no technical or statutory support in the ITA or the ITR for netting sales revenue against qualifying SR&ED expenditures. In Canadian tax law, whether an activity constitutes SR&ED—a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis—is to be determined objectively, irrespective of what is done with the resulting product, whether it be sold, stored, or scrapped. If an expenditure satisfies paragraph 37(1)(a) of the ITA and section 2900 of the ITR, the subsequent incidental realization of revenue from selling the physical output of that experiment does not retroactively alter the nature of the expenditure.

Furthermore, Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. exposed the accounting vulnerability that later materialized in Consoltex Inc. as the "carve-out" method. Under the carve-out theory, when a taxpayer sells products generated during SR&ED trials, the tax authority attempts to extract the accounting "cost of sales" (raw materials, direct labour, and factory overhead attributed to inventory under section 9 and section 10 of the ITA) from the section 37 SR&ED pool. While the Tax Court of Canada rejected both arbitrary revenue netting in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. and formulaic cost-of-sales carve-outs in Consoltex Inc., taxpayers whose financial accounting systems book experimental trial runs directly into commercial Work-in-Process (WIP) or Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) ledgers invite immediate audit disallowance. Separately, Parliament later introduced investment tax credit recapture rules (subsections 127(27) to (36) of the ITA), intended to ensure that only the net cost of performing SR&ED attracts SR&ED tax incentives where property that generated an ITC is disposed of or converted to commercial use, making precise cost segregation between research and inventory even more vital for modern Canadian claimants.
Deficiencies in Proportional Cost Allocation and Clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A) / Paragraph 2902(b) Compliance

The second major evidentiary friction point in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. involved the proportional allocation of the appellant's capital expenditures between eligible SR&ED and production, under subsection 127(9) of the ITA and paragraph 2902(b) of the ITR, which treats capital expenditures in respect of the acquisition of property as prescribed (and thus excluded from qualified expenditures) unless they were incurred for and all or substantially all attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED. Because the appellant had indicated that 80 percent of its current expenditures were incurred for research—a percentage taken from its own financial statements and accepted by Revenue Canada—the Minister concluded that the same percentage should apply to its capital expenditures and that the facilities were therefore not all or substantially all devoted to SR&ED but were in fact used for production.

When a taxpayer claims a block of current operational expenses without maintaining granular, contemporaneous project cost accounting that tracks each employee's hours, specific square footage of experimental chambers, and exact substrate batches back to distinct SR&ED hypotheses, the CRA invokes the "all or substantially all" and "directly attributable" requirements of clauses 37(7)(c)(ii)(A) and (B) of the ITA (today found in subsection 37(8) of the ITA). Under clause (A), an expenditure qualifies if "all or substantially all" (90 percent or more) of the outlay was attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED, while under clause (B) and subsection 2900(2) of the ITR, current expenditures directly attributable to SR&ED—such as materials consumed and a reasonable allocation of salaries—qualify, separately from general business overhead and prescribed expenditures under paragraph 2902(a) of the ITR. In Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc., the Court did not need to adjudicate the proportion of current expenditures, which was agreed at 80 percent; rather, it held that the Minister could not simply transpose that percentage to the capital expenditures, because the uncontradicted testimony of the appellant's president established that the capital expenditures claimed as qualified were all incurred for the purposes of the research laboratory, so that the percentage applied by the Minister was not based on the facts.
Evidentiary Burden in Proving Technological Uncertainty in Biological and Process Engineering

Although technological uncertainty was not litigated in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc.—Revenue Canada recognized, and the Minister did not question, that the appellant conducted SR&ED within the meaning of the Regulations—its factual matrix illustrates a recurring evidentiary challenge: the difficulty of proving technological uncertainty and systematic experimentation in biological, agricultural, and shop-floor process industries under section 2900 of the ITR. To an external reviewer, installing metal slats inside a building and placing wooden logs inside perforated plastic bags to grow oyster mushrooms can easily be misconstrued as routine agricultural facility optimization or standard horticultural practice.

For such activities to qualify as experimental development under section 2900 of the ITR, the taxpayer bears the legal burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that standard practice and publicly available mycological or environmental engineering knowledge could not predict how the interaction of metal-slat thermal and humidity conductivity and specific plastic perforation geometries would affect spore germination, mycelial colonization, and contamination rates on wood-log substrates. Without contemporaneous experimental protocols detailing baseline control parameters, specific quantitative hypotheses, environmental sensor logs, and biological yield or contamination analyses, taxpayers in biological or process manufacturing sectors routinely fail to establish that their physical modifications constitute a "systematic investigation or search" rather than routine commercial troubleshooting.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement relevant to Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. against the specific operational or administrative issue that arose in, or is illustrated by, the litigation and the position taken by the Tax Court of Canada (and, in the final row, in Consoltex Inc.).

headers: Taxpayer Operational Vulnerability or Crown Legal Error
Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof and Judicial Holding

cells: Systematic Investigation & Technological Advancement (ITR Section 2900)

Conducting a biological and agricultural experimental process (controlling and limiting the spread of oyster mushroom spores using interior metal slats and wood logs in perforated plastic bags) whose output was sold invited the Minister's argument that the appellant was in a commercial production phase.

Not in dispute: Revenue Canada recognized that the appellant conducted SR&ED. The Court rejected the Minister's reliance on paragraph 2900(h), holding that the same expenditures cannot be related both to the scientific research phase and to a commercial production phase.
Current Expenditures Incurred "On" SR&ED (ITA Paragraph 37(1)(a) & Clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A))

The appellant's activities were allocated in its financial statements as 80 percent research; Revenue Canada accepted that 80 percent of current expenditures ($85,104) related to research and development, so no dispute arose over the current-expenditure proportion.

The current-expenditure proportion was not adjudicated and the s. 37 deductions were not contested; the Court refused to allow the Minister to extend that 80 percent proportion to a different category of expenditure (capital expenditures) where the evidence showed otherwise.
Exclusion of Prescribed Expenditures (ITA Subsection 127(9) & ITR Paragraph 2902(b))

The Minister excluded the appellant's capital expenditures (up to $34,777) from the "qualified expenditure" base as prescribed expenditures under paragraph 2902(b), applying the 80 percent current-expenditure proportion and alleging the property was used for production.

The uncontradicted testimony of the appellant's president established that the capital expenditures claimed as qualified were all incurred for the purposes of the research laboratory; the Minister's percentage was not based on the facts and could not be considered valid.
Gross Qualifying Expenditure Integrity vs. "Netting" of Sales Proceeds (ITA Subsections 37(1), 127(5), and 127(9))

Because oyster mushrooms grown during experimental trials were sold commercially, Revenue Canada applied an extrastatutory administrative policy ("netting") to reduce qualifying SR&ED expenditures by the gross proceeds of sale.

Appeal Allowed with Costs: The ITA contains no provision requiring or authorizing the reduction ("netting") of qualified expenditures of a current nature by the sums received from the sale of experimental products, as counsel for the Minister conceded. Where Parliament wished to reduce qualified expenditures it said so expressly in s. 127(11.1) (government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments, which do not include payments for experimental products), and the Minister's object-of-the-Act, matching, and s. 2900(h) arguments were rejected.
Rejection of the "Carve-Out" Corollary (Cultures Laflamme as applied in Consoltex Inc.)

Tax authorities sought to attribute a portion of the SR&ED costs to the accounting "cost of sales" of commercially sold experimental output (the "carve-out" approach), as an alternative to netting gross sales revenue.

Expressly agreeing with Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. on netting, the Tax Court held that the carve-out approach—superficially resembling netting but based on a different premise—does not conform to the scheme and purpose of the SR&ED provisions: the expenditures can be SR&ED expenditures and also form part of the cost of inventory, and the disposition of the product does not change the nature of the activity.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles of Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. (and its companion precedent Consoltex Inc.) into actionable compliance strategies under current CRA administrative guidelines—including the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (which applies the ED+EP / ED+CP framework and succeeded the former Experimental Production and Commercial Production with Experimental Development Work application policy) and the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives (which replaced the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy in 2021)—the following two industry case studies demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers can proactively structure their operations to defeat audit challenges.
Case Study 1: Controlled-Environment Mycological and Bioprocessing Facility (Agri-Tech Sector)
Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

Laurentian MycoTech Inc., a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) based in Drummondville, Quebec, cultivates specialty culinary and medicinal fungi (Pleurotus ostreatus and Hericium erinaceus) sold to wholesale grocery distributors across Canada. In its 2026 taxation year, Laurentian MycoTech initiates an R&D project to overcome a severe biological and environmental engineering limitation: standard lignocellulosic hardwood logs and sawdust blocks encased in conventional micro-perforated polypropylene bags suffer a 38 percent mycelial die-off and Trichoderma green-mould contamination rate when scaled inside high-density vertical growth rooms lined with anodized aluminum radiant cooling panels. To resolve this technological obstacle, the company modifies two of its six commercial growing zones with custom-engineered corrugated aluminum-zinc alloy wall slats and tests 14 permutations of laser-perforated biodegradable polymer substrate bags across 12,000 inoculated hardwood logs. Because the uncontaminated logs in the two experimental zones produce marketable fruiting bodies, Laurentian MycoTech harvests those mushrooms and sells them alongside its regular commercial crop for $420,000, while claiming $650,000 in current SR&ED expenditures comprising mycologists' salaries, facility climate-control utilities, substrate logs, perforated bags, and technician labour.

Without proactive structural remediation, Laurentian MycoTech faces audit risks that echo, and extend beyond, the two issues litigated in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. (the netting of experimental sales proceeds and the "all or substantially all" allocation of expenditures). First, the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) will allege that growing mushrooms in Zones 1 and 2 constitutes routine commercial production or trial-and-error horticulture excluded under the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA (formerly section 2900 of the ITR). Second, the CRA Financial Reviewer (FR) will challenge the mixed facility utility and technician wage claims under subsection 37(8) of the ITA (the successor to former paragraph 37(7)(c)) and paragraph 2902(a) of the ITR, arguing that the expenses represent general commercial overhead not incurred "all or substantially all" for SR&ED. Third, the CRA FR will attempt to disallow the substrate, bag, and direct harvesting labour costs as commercial Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) or reduce the qualifying expenditure pool by the $420,000 of mushroom sales proceeds through an administrative netting or carve-out adjustment.
Step-by-Step Restructuring of Project Governance

To neutralize these vulnerabilities at the governance level, Laurentian MycoTech must establish an internal SR&ED Governance Committee prior to initiating any physical modifications in Zones 1 and 2. The committee must formally charter the project through an Experimental Development Project Authorization Resolution that legally and operationally separates the mandate of the two experimental zones from the four commercial production zones. Under this governance protocol, Zones 1 and 2 are officially designated as "Quarantined Experimental Bioprocessing Bays" for the defined 36-week duration of the experimental campaign. The governance charter must explicitly record that the primary corporate objective of every inoculation cycle in Bays 1 and 2 is the generation of scientific and engineering data to resolve the technological uncertainty surrounding radiative heat transfer from the metal wall slats and gaseous mass-transfer kinetics across the perforated bag boundary layer, rather than the fulfillment of commercial customer purchase orders. Any edible biomass recovered at the conclusion of an experimental measurement cycle is formally classified in corporate minutes as "Incidental Experimental By-Product Biomass" rather than scheduled commercial production.
Step-by-Step Restructuring of Technical Documentation

To satisfy the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA (formerly section 2900 of the ITR) and prevent the CRA from characterizing the metal slats and perforated plastic bags as routine facility upgrades, Laurentian MycoTech must structure its contemporaneous technical documentation around the systematic investigation standard that Revenue Canada accepted had been met in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc.. Prior to installing a single metal slat or wrapping a single log, the lead mycologist must author a Baseline Technological Limitation Brief documenting why existing psychrometric models and commercial mycological manuals cannot predict condensation nucleation and convective boundary-layer stagnation when radiant metal wall slats interact with respiratory metabolic heat generated inside perforated log bags. Thereafter, each of the 14 experimental runs must be governed by a pre-registered Experimental Protocol Sheet stating a testable, quantitative hypothesis that correlates specific slat fin-angles and micro-perforation pore densities (measured in micrometres, from 80 to 500 µm) against internal substrate core temperatures and mycelial colonization rates. Crucially, to prove that the inoculated logs serve as experimental apparatus rather than commercial inventory, the technical protocol must mandate destructive core sampling on a statistically significant subset of logs in every batch to measure internal moisture gradients, pH shifts, and microscopic hyphal density, paired with continuous data-logging of psychrometric sensors affixed directly to the interior metal slats.
Step-by-Step Restructuring of Contract Terms and Commercial Sales Accounting

To insulate the $650,000 SR&ED expenditure claim from any CRA attempt to revive the "netting" or "carve-out" doctrines rejected in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. and Consoltex Inc., Laurentian MycoTech must decouple its commercial sales contracts from its experimental trials. All recurring commercial supply agreements with grocery distributors must be contractually ring-fenced so that delivery obligations are fulfilled exclusively from the baseline capacity of Commercial Zones 3 through 6. No distributor contract may stipulate financial contributions toward, or guaranteed delivery from, Experimental Bays 1 and 2, thereby avoiding both paragraph 37(1)(d) government or non-government assistance reductions and "contract payment" exclusions under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. When uncontaminated oyster mushrooms from Experimental Bays 1 and 2 survive destructive sampling and are sold on the spot wholesale market for $420,000, the accounting department must record those proceeds in a segregated general ledger revenue account titled Account 4900 – Incidental Proceeds from Sale of Experimental Production (Taxable per ITA s. 9). Consistent with Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc., which held that sums received from the sale of experimental products are not deducted in calculating qualified expenditures, zero dollars are netted against Form T661 qualifying expenditures, while the $420,000 is included in full in computing business income under section 9 of the ITA. Furthermore, the input costs of the experimental logs and perforated bags must never pass through the commercial Inventory or Cost of Goods Sold accounts, preventing any audit allegation of a double deduction under section 9 and section 37 of the ITA.
Step-by-Step Restructuring of Experimentation and Cost-Allocation Tracking

To preempt an allocation dispute of the kind that required judicial intervention in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc.—where the Minister transposed the 80 percent current-expenditure proportion to the capital expenditures under paragraph 2902(b) of the ITR—and to satisfy paragraph 37(1)(a), subsection 37(8) of the ITA, and paragraph 2902(a) of the ITR, Laurentian MycoTech must implement a dual-layer project accounting architecture. Whether electing the contemporary Proxy Method or the Traditional Method (as was in force during the 1986 taxation year adjudicated in Cultures Laflamme), the company must install dedicated electrical and HVAC sub-meters on Experimental Bays 1 and 2 and issue separate vendor purchase orders for the 12,000 experimental hardwood logs and laser-perforated bags coded directly to an isolated SR&ED project cost centre. This physical and accounting segregation establishes 100 percent ("all or substantially all") attribution for materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED. Simultaneously, rather than relying on an end-of-year management estimate of the proportion of time spent on research versus commercial harvesting, all mycologists and facility technicians must log daily hours using biometric badge-swipe task codes that separate eligible SR&ED activities (experimental setup, slat calibration, spore inoculation, sensor monitoring, and destructive mycological analysis) from ineligible commercial work (Commercial Zone 3–6 cultivation and post-trial commercial packaging). By voluntarily excluding the post-trial labour incurred purely to package and ship the surviving experimental mushrooms to market, Laurentian MycoTech renders its remaining SR&ED labour and current expenditure claim impregnable on audit.
Case Study 2: Full-Scale Mill Trials in Specialty Polymer-Coated Technical Textiles (Advanced Manufacturing Sector)
Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

ekoWeave Composites Ltd., an industrial textile manufacturer located in Granby, Quebec, produces high-tenacity woven aramid and polyester fabrics. During its 2026 taxation year, ekoWeave undertakes an experimental development project to formulate a novel fluoropolymer-free, bio-based polyurethane dispersion (PUD) sizing and finishing process capable of withstanding high-speed air-jet loom abrasion at 1,100 picks per minute while imparting hydrostatic flame resistance. Because laboratory bench-scale coaters cannot replicate the dynamic warp-yarn tension, harmonic vibration, and thermal curing shear experienced across a 3.2-metre industrial weaving beam during the four sequential operations of beaming or warping, slashing or sizing, entering through the heddles, and weaving, ekoWeave must conduct 28 full-scale experimental trial runs directly on its main commercial production looms. Across these 28 trials, ekoWeave expends $1,150,000 in warp and filling yarn, experimental chemical dispersions, polymers, and mill engineering and operator labour. Twenty-one of the 28 experimental runs produce woven fabric rolls that—while failing the target aerospace flame-retardancy threshold—meet secondary commercial specifications for industrial tarpaulins. ekoWeave sells those trial rolls to commercial textile jobbers for $1,300,000, resulting in gross sales proceeds that exceed the $1,150,000 SR&ED expenditure claim.

This industrial scenario replicates the exact legal nexus joining Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. and Consoltex Inc.. On audit, the CRA will contend that because the trials took place inside commercial production facilities on production looms and generated $1,300,000 in sales revenue (wiping out the $1,150,000 R&D expenditure if netted), the entire activity constituted commercial production accompanied by routine trial-and-error adjustments. Alternatively, relying on its administrative SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (treating the runs as experimental development in conjunction with commercial production, or ED+CP), the CRA will attempt to disallow the yarn and loom operating costs by asserting that only the incremental non-recoverable cost qualifies, effectively resurrecting the netting approach rejected by Judge Lamarre Proulx in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. and the netting and carve-out approaches—including the argument that only the marginal cost of producing the fabric in the course of SR&ED qualifies—rejected by Judge Bowman in Consoltex Inc..
Step-by-Step Restructuring of Project Governance

To overcome the presumption of commercial production on the shop floor, ekoWeave must institute a formal Shop-Floor Trial Governance Protocol that governs every transition of a commercial loom from standard manufacturing to SR&ED experimental development. Under this governance regime, a production loom cannot be utilized for an SR&ED trial without a signed Engineering Trial Loom Takeover Directive jointly executed by the Vice-President of R&D and the Plant Operations Director prior to beaming. Crucially, the governance directive must establish and technically justify the Minimum Experimental Batch Size (MEBS) required to test the hypothesis. In industrial textile processing, large lengths of fabric may be needed before problems are identified and solved—in Consoltex Inc., several hundred metres had to be woven between each loom adjustment in one project and 52,000 metres were ultimately produced in another—so the charter must document the minimum batch length (for example, 1,500 linear metres of parallel warp yarns) needed to achieve steady-state mechanical tension through the chemical slashing bath, drying cylinders, heddle frames, and weaving loom. By documenting in the project charter prior to the run that a 1,500-metre batch is dictated strictly by the physical and mechanical engineering constraints of the beaming, slashing, entering, and weaving equipment—and not by commercial order volume—ekoWeave establishes as a matter of evidentiary fact that the entire run is an experimental trial rather than commercial production with incidental testing.
Step-by-Step Restructuring of Technical Documentation

To prove that the 28 full-scale mill runs constitute a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" under the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA (formerly section 2900 of the ITR), ekoWeave's technical documentation must establish a rigorous causal link between the chemical-mechanical uncertainty and each shop-floor run. Before each warp beam is wound and passed through the chemical slashing bath, the R&D engineering team must record a Pre-Run Chemical and Mechanical Parameter Matrix specifying the exact rheological formulation of the bio-based polymer bath, cross-linking catalyst ratios, drying cylinder thermal profiles, and loom warp-tension settings, accompanied by an engineering analysis explaining why the abrasion and flame-retardancy outcome of that specific formulation could not be predicted from prior runs or polymer science literature. During the weaving operation, automated loom telemetry and R&D personnel must compile In-Line Stop-Motion and Yarn-Breakage Logs recording warp-break frequencies per 10,000 picks, size-film flaking rates on the heddles, and polymer adhesion anomalies during converting and finishing. Following each run, every trial roll must undergo destructive tensile, abrasion, and cone-calorimeter flame testing in the laboratory, with the empirical results synthesized into an Experimental Iteration Post-Mortem Report that dictates the systematic chemical reformulation for the subsequent trial run.
Step-by-Step Restructuring of Contract Terms and Commercial Sales Accounting

To defeat any CRA attempt to apply revenue netting or cost-of-sales carve-outs against the $1,150,000 SR&ED claim, ekoWeave must structure the commercial disposition of the 21 salable trial rolls with strict legal and accounting precision. First, corporate policy must prohibit initiating any of the 28 experimental runs against an open customer purchase order or custom-fabric development contract; if a trial roll is woven to fulfill an existing customer order, the CRA can credibly argue that the primary purpose of the outlay was commercial inventory fulfilment rather than SR&ED. Only after the R&D department has completed its destructive laboratory sampling and executed a formal Technical Release of Experimental Prototype Material may the surviving fabric yardage be transferred to the commercial sales team for liquidation to secondary textile jobbers. All sales contracts and commercial invoices issued to those jobbers must explicitly designate the goods as Experimental Trial Lots – Sold As-Is / Secondary Specification.

In the corporation's financial statements and T2 corporate income tax return, the $1,300,000 received from the jobbers is recognized in full as taxable gross business revenue under section 9 of the ITA. Simultaneously, because the $1,150,000 of yarn, chemicals, and direct trial labour was expensed directly into the section 37 SR&ED pool (Account 7500 – Direct SR&ED Experimental Production Costs), those outlays are completely excluded from commercial inventory valuation under section 10 of the ITA and from Cost of Goods Sold. Consequently, the accounting cost of sales for the salvaged trial rolls for section 9 purposes is zero, ensuring that the entire $1,300,000 sales price flows into taxable business income while the full $1,150,000 expenditure qualifies for the section 37 deduction and subsection 127(5) Investment Tax Credits without any netting or carve-out reduction, consistent with the rejection of netting in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. and of both netting and carve-out in Consoltex Inc..
Step-by-Step Restructuring of Experimentation and Cost-Allocation Tracking

Finally, to reflect the evidence-based allocation standard applied by Judge Lamarre Proulx in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. (which rejected a percentage transposed from one category of expenditure to another without a factual basis) and current ITA subsections 37(1) and 127(9), ekoWeave must implement a segregated Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) shop-floor tracking protocol. Standard commercial weaving runs must be executed under commercial work orders that capitalize raw yarn, sizing chemicals, and direct weaving labour into WIP Inventory under section 9 and section 10 of the ITA. Conversely, whenever an Engineering Trial Loom Takeover Directive is active, the ERP system must generate a dedicated experimental work order that routes all raw materials and direct operator and engineer hours directly to the section 37 SR&ED expenditure ledger.

Furthermore, to account for post-Cultures Laflamme statutory amendments to the ITA governing the recapture of Investment Tax Credits on SR&ED property sold or converted to commercial use, ekoWeave's ERP work orders must precisely demarcate Materials Consumed from Materials Transformed. The exact linear yardage of the 7 completely destroyed trial runs, the warp waste removed during slashing and entering, and the destructively tested laboratory swatches cut from the 21 surviving runs must be tracked and claimed as Materials Consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED (which are permanently exempt from ITC recapture). Meanwhile, the raw material cost of the yarn and polymer physically embedded in the net yardage of the 21 sold rolls is tracked separately as Materials Transformed, allowing the taxpayer to comply seamlessly with modern statutory material recapture rules on the embedded raw fibre cost while preserving 100 percent of its SR&ED engineering salaries, loom operator trial wages, overhead proxy, and consumed material expenditures completely free from any revenue netting or cost-of-sales carve-out.

body.text: Conclusion and Strategic Takeaways for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The decision of Judge Louise Lamarre Proulx in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. v. Minister of National Revenue remains a vital pillar of Canadian SR&ED tax jurisprudence. By establishing that the Income Tax Act does not require the sums received from the sale of experimental products to be deducted in calculating qualified SR&ED expenditures, and by holding that the Minister could not transpose the 80 percent proportion of current expenditures to capital expenditures that the uncontradicted evidence showed were all incurred for the research laboratory, the Tax Court of Canada safeguarded the statutory integrity of the investment tax credit under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) for Canadian industrial and agricultural innovators. When combined with proactive project governance, hypothesis-driven technical documentation, strict separation of commercial order fulfilment from experimental runs, and granular ERP cost accounting, the legal principles articulated in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. empower Canadian taxpayers to conduct full-scale experimental development inside commercial facilities without forfeiting their statutory SR&ED tax incentives.
